name: Nikhil Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a reablement team, which means I help people for the first six weeks after they come home from hospital, so they can do things for themselves again. The agency I work for, Pathway Care, has the contract with the hospital trust. So one morning I'm helping a man who's had a hip replacement practise getting into the bath, and in the afternoon I'm making toast alongside a lady after a stroke so she can learn to do it one-handed. I like that people get better, which you don't always see in care. What wears me out is when they discharge someone too early and we're picking up the pieces.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the money side look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not great, not terrible. The rate's lower than the big agencies, because Pathway undercut them to win the contract. I've got about two and a half weeks' worth in savings and a car loan with eighteen months left. My girlfriend Sana works on reception at a dental surgery, so between us we manage the rent on a two-bed in the new estate by the ring road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's the boring one, but boring's not bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably for the best, a lot of the hype was always overdone. I'd say the useful bits are fine, like the app that reminds people to take their tablets. I'm not going to rant about it either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means the money stays tight. The contract with the trust gets re-tendered every three years, and My agency won the hospital contract by being cheapest, so they'll squeeze us again to keep it. Two and a half weeks of savings isn't much if they cut the rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the reablement work, because I'm good at it and the physios ask for me. I'd use the chat AI now and then to plan meals for diabetic clients, like I do already. And I'd overpay the car loan by twenty a month to get it gone sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A small worry about the next tender, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the physios ask for you. Does that count for anything at Pathway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in money. It counts for which shifts I get, though. I get the interesting cases instead of the fifteen-minute sit-and-check calls, and that keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Pathway cut the rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd see what the other carers did. If everyone stayed, I'd probably stay, there's not much else round here. If a few went to the hospital bank staff, I'd ask them how it was.

I'd say I'm **not going to rant** about it either way.
think: Privately the money **stays tight** whatever AI does.
Pathway won the contract by being **cheapest**, so they'll squeeze pay at re-tender.
do: Keep doing **reablement work**, where physios ask for him.
Use the chat AI to **plan meals** for diabetic clients.
Overpay the **car loan** by twenty a month.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with a small worry about the **next tender**.

fieldNote: His concern is the **contract re-tender**, a pressure that exists without AI.
He takes his cue from **what others do**, fitting his steady style.
He gets **satisfaction** from clients recovering, rare in care work.

steps.text: Keep doing reablement visits with the hospital physios
Plan diabetic clients' meals with the chat AI
Overpay the car loan by twenty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking and answering customers. That's Sana's whole job, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be a big change for office people and less for us on the ground. I'd say carers should be fine for a while. I'd share some of the practical stuff, like which apps actually help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm okay, but Sana's job is right in the firing line. My girlfriend Sana does booking, phones and chasing payments at a dental surgery, and that's exactly what AI does first. If she goes down to part-time, we can't make rent on what I earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Sana this month and look at what she could move into, maybe a dental nurse course, because that's hands-on. I'd try the AI tool that writes the reablement progress notes, once the others on my team say it saves time. And we'd stop eating out on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for me, worried for her. It's strange when the threat's to the other person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you think Sana would react to that conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say she already knows, because the surgery's already trialling an online booking system. She'd probably be annoyed I raised it first. But she'd look at the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your team leader about the notes tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd try it if it saves us real time, not just more boxes to tick. Our team leader Joanne's practical, she'd want proof too. We'd probably trial it for a month.

say: I'd say it's a **big change** for **office people**, less for carers.
think: I think **Sana's reception job** is right in the firing line.
If she goes **part-time**, we can't make rent on my pay.

Try the AI **progress notes tool** once colleagues say it works.

fieldNote: His own hands-on job feels safe; the **household risk** is Sana's desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. 2028. That's really soon. And robots three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government, quickly, because two years isn't enough for anyone. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it. I'd probably sign petitions, that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my girlfriend Sana's job goes in 2028 and mine lasts until about 2031, so that's three years of us living on one low wage. Robots that can help someone into a bath show up around then, and after that maybe there's no wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, we'd move to a cheaper one-bed to cut the rent by maybe a hundred and fifty. I'd look at physiotherapy assistant jobs at the hospital, because they mix hands-on with judgement. And I'd pick up extra weekend shifts while the work's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I'm usually the calm one, and I'm not calm about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sana's parents, who you're close to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're okay for now, even if we weren't. Her dad would offer money, he always does. I'd probably take it this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a physio assistant job safer than yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. There's more deciding and explaining, but AI would do the deciding by 2028. Honestly, I don't know. It's just the closest thing I could get into fast.

I'd **sign petitions** asking for support for families like ours.
think: I think **Sana's job goes** almost straight away, in 2028.

He admits a physio assistant job is **only slightly safer**.

steps.text: Move to a cheaper one-bed flat to cut rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's still quick, but it's something you can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now, and that employers should help. I'd say it at work, mostly, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it gives Sana time to finish a dental nurse course before 2031, which is the big thing. My job goes around 2034, so I'd have time to try something, maybe the physio assistant route. We'd still be stretched, but we'd have options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Sana sign up for the dental nurse course next September. I'd start building savings, aiming for two months by 2030. And I'd ask Joanne about shadowing the hospital physios on my days off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but more like before exams than before a crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two months' savings by 2030: how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the car loan's paid off, that's a hundred and ten a month freed up, and we'd just keep living like it's still there. That gets us there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI more to get ready?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, once I've seen it do something useful. I'd use it to learn the anatomy for physio work. I wouldn't trust it to plan my life, though.

fieldNote: Five years turns fear into a **two-person training plan**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to change jobs twice if you had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, but don't waste it. I'd say government and employers should fund training now, while it's cheap to do. Calm, sensible stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think we'd be fine if we use it. Sana could be a dental nurse by 2029 and I could be a physio assistant or even study for a physio degree. The worry is that we don't, because ten years feels like forever and then it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd pay off the car loan and start saving. I'd look at a part-time access course for a physio degree, and see how others on it find it. Sana would look at the dental course too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Like there's a path, if we actually walk it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think you'd actually walk it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sana would make sure I did. She's more organised than me. I'm the one who'd put it off until next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your clients in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope there's still a person checking the robot got the bath right. Maybe that's me, at forty. Somebody has to know when a hip patient's scared, not just weak.

I'd ask government and employers to **fund training now**, while it's cheap to do.
think: I think we'd be **fine if we use** the time.
The risk is that ten years **feels like forever**, until it isn't.

Look at a part-time **access course** for a physio degree.
Encourage Sana to start the **dental course**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sana's job would go almost at once and mine wouldn't be far behind. What would help is free retraining for people on low pay, and some help with rent during the gap, so you don't lose your home while you're learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the hospital discharges. Even now, people come home from hospital too early, and that's not AI, that's beds.

headlineQuote: People come home from hospital too early, and that's not AI, that's beds.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old reablement carer** helping people recover at home after hospital.
He has **thin savings** of about two and a half weeks, a car loan, and shares rent with Sana.
His biggest AI worry is **Sana's dental reception job**, which is exposed to thinking AI.
He takes up tools **once colleagues prove them**, and plans steadily with longer warning.
With time, he aims for **physiotherapy work**; with two years, he'd move somewhere cheaper.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with Sana's job going at once and his soon after.
whatWouldHelp: **Free retraining** for low-paid workers and **rent help** during the gap.
